source: Johnson (1987) Knowledge and skill differences between expert and novice service technicians on technical troubleshooting tasks
finding: Study 1 compared 5 novices and 5 experts on generator sets. Experts knew basic principles and system function much better. Novices lacked an accurate mental model of equipment they repair daily.
numbers: Novices averaged about 0.5 year repairing generators; experts averaged over 10 years. N=5 vs 5. Schematic tracing of battery, ground and AC circuits: experts significantly more accurate on all three (exact test values garbled in the scan).
quote: novices seem to lack an accurate mental model of the operation of the technical systems they repair daily
limits: Tiny sample; the scan hides some test statistics. Experts were factory staff, novices were trainees, so experience and role are mixed.
agent_relevance: Expertise is a system model, not a longer rule list. S0 memory should hold a device model, not only past cases.

source: Johnson (1987) Knowledge and skill differences between expert and novice service technicians on technical troubleshooting tasks
finding: Study 2 used think-aloud on two rare faults (fuel pump, open wire). All experts found both faults. Novices did not.
numbers: Experts 5/5 on both. Novices: fuel pump 3/5, open wire 2/5. Cutoff 45 min; only 1 of 5 failures hit the time limit, so novices mostly gave up. Open-wire (electrical) task: experts about 5 times faster. Fuel-pump (mechanical) task: novices who solved it were faster than experts.
quote: On the wire problem, experts solved it almost five times faster than novices.
limits: Domain match matters: novices had mechanical but not electrical experience. Only 2 problems, 10 people.
agent_relevance: Expertise is domain-bound. Do not assume a schema from one device transfers to another.

source: Johnson (1987) Knowledge and skill differences between expert and novice service technicians on technical troubleshooting tasks
finding: Experts read more from the first symptom and built a correct problem space. Novices formed no explicit starting picture and searched by trial and error.
numbers: Expert 1 inferred battery, fuse and board were good from the fuel pump clicking. Novice 1 said only: I get nothing, I am just going to look around. Most expert checks fell inside the true problem space; novices made many hypotheses outside it.
quote: I can feel the fuel pump pumping so I know that I do have voltage to my fuel pump.
limits: Qualitative; two problems; maps drawn by the author.
agent_relevance: Matches our S1-S2: state the symptom and what it already rules out before any test (G1, G2).

source: Johnson (1987) Knowledge and skill differences between expert and novice service technicians on technical troubleshooting tasks
finding: Experts chose technical tests; novices chose sensory checks (sight, sound, smell, touch). Test skill itself did not differ.
numbers: Experts relied on test procedures more; no difference in how accurately the chosen tests were done. Novice information seldom shrank the problem space.
limits: Qualitative coding; no counts given in the surviving text.
agent_relevance: Quality of the chosen test, not skill at running it, separates experts. Put effort in test selection (S4).

source: Johnson (1995) Understanding troubleshooting styles to improve training methods
finding: A review of over fifty troubleshooters over eight years. Strategy type did not separate high from low performers. Range of strategies did.
numbers: Five strategies named: trial and error, exhaustive, topographic, half/split, functional. Low performers in Johnson et al. 1993 were strategy bound; skilled ones used several and even reverted to trial and error when stuck.
quote: The highest performing troubleshooters are masters of many different troubleshooting strategies.
limits: Secondary summary of Johnson et al. 1993 and others; no raw numbers for this point.
agent_relevance: Supports a small set of operators with switching on impasse (O1-O8), not one fixed method.

source: Johnson (1995) Understanding troubleshooting styles to improve training methods (citing Johnson, Flesher, Jehng & Ferej 1993)
finding: Theory knowledge did not predict troubleshooting skill in a student study. High and low performers scored the same on a systems exam.
numbers: Systems post-test (max 24): high performers 19.82 (SD 1.94), low performers 19.88 (SD 2.13); t(32)=0.073, p>.05. University students after an avionics course.
limits: Students, not workers; N about 34. Absence of a difference is not proof of none. Conflicts in part with Johnson 1987, where experts did know principles better.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: knowing the theory is not the same as using it. A model that can recite physics may still diagnose badly.

source: Johnson (1995) Understanding troubleshooting styles to improve training methods
finding: Both groups kept their first frame and rarely checked other subsystems, even when cued. Experts and novices interpreted found information about equally well.
numbers: Concept-map study: concept maps raised behavioural understanding (Mann-Whitney U=2.50, p<.01) but not structure knowledge; flow diagrams gave more expert-like knowledge maps (t(82)=-4.705, p<.01).
quote: subjects rarely questioned the initial reference frame they had established
limits: Review; effects are for training formats, not expertise itself.
agent_relevance: Anchoring on the first frame hits experts too. This is the case for G1 (doubt on a signal) plus a forced check of untested subsystems.

source: Lesgold, Lajoie, Bunzo & Eggan (1988) Sherlock: a coached practice environment for an electronics troubleshooting job
finding: Task analysis of Air Force test-station repair. Experts split the space; trainees traced circuits end to end. What differs with expertise is which space is split.
numbers: Expert solved the sample problem in 7 steps; trainees took 14 and 20. The station breaks about once a month; routine work is about 95% of the job, so novices get little practice at the hard 5%.
quote: What differs with expertise is the space that is split when space splitting strategies are employed.
limits: One worked example, not a sample; trainees were selected as high promise.
agent_relevance: Space-splitting is only as good as the model it splits. Models that split by swappable cards waste effort versus splitting by function (S2, S4).

source: Steinberg & Gitomer (1992) Cognitive task analysis, interface design, and technical troubleshooting (HYDRIVE)
finding: PARI task analysis of F-15 hydraulics technicians from novice to expert listed the skills that differ.
numbers: Seven differences: attend to physical clues; explicit accurate mental models; procedural expertise (disabling systems to rule out areas); hierarchical functional classification of components; knowledge of failure characteristics; flexible strategy with space splitting; cost/benefit awareness. Novices are limited to remove-and-replace.
quote: The ability to balance cost and information is one of the hallmarks of expertise in this domain.
limits: Descriptive; sample size of technicians not stated in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Direct list for the schema: model, classification, failure priors, cost-aware information gain. Cost-aware test choice is the mark of expertise.

source: Katz et al. (1997) Cognitive task analysis and intelligent computer-based training systems: lessons learned from Sherlock, Hydrive and Eagle Keeper
finding: Three kinds of knowledge underlie avionics expertise: conceptual, strategic, procedural. Procedure did not separate experts from novices in hydraulics. Strategy and system knowledge did.
numbers: Hydrive (task-analysis informed, teaches strategy) vs F-15 Pneudraulics tutor (procedure focus) vs control: only Hydrive improved, t(19)=4.14, p<.001. Gains came on problems with no fault-isolation guide.
limits: Conference slide text; the earlier tutor also differed in other ways than CTA.
agent_relevance: Teach and prompt strategy and system model, not procedures. Procedures can be given by lookup; strategy has to be in the schema.

source: Katz et al. (1997) Sherlock field evaluation, as summarised
finding: About 20 hours on Sherlock over 3 weeks lifted novices to master level on trained tests.
numbers: Tutored n=18, untutored n=23, masters n=13 (4+ times the job experience). Posttest VTT3 t[39]=-4.04, VTT4 t[39]=-3.72, both p<.001, tutored comparable to masters. Frankenstation (novel station): tutored n=17, untutored n=21, masters n=12; t[36]=-2.93, p<.01.
limits: Verbal test scored by experts; tests partly built from the same task analysis as the tutor.
agent_relevance: Experience can be compressed when the expert model is the training target. Same logic as giving an agent the expert schema directly.

source: Gott group (1995) Tutoring for transfer of technical competence (Sherlock 2 evaluation)
finding: Controlled study of 54 airmen at three bases. Tutored novices matched master technicians on trained tests.
numbers: Posttests mean (SD). Control N=23: VTT3 59 (37), VTT4 58 (37), NIT 75 (14). Tutored N=18: 95 (5), 91 (7), 87 (12). Masters N=13: 85 (12), 86 (11), 86 (11). Effect sizes 1.27, 1.17, 0.87 SD. Pretest: masters beat novices on VTT t=-2.81 p=.007 and NIT t=-3.03 p=.004; no aptitude gap.
quote: Effect sizes 1.27, 1.17, 0.87 SD vs 0.3 SD for typical school curricula (Bloom 1984).
limits: Control SD is large (37) so the control mean is unstable. Tutored group scored above masters on trained tests. Partial results of a larger report.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that coaching on an expert model closes much of the expert-novice gap.

source: Gott group (1995) Tutoring for transfer of technical competence: Frankenstation transfer test
finding: Tutored novices transferred to an unfamiliar computer-controlled test station. Controls did not.
numbers: Frankenstation VTT: control N=21 mean 55 (SD 31); tutored N=17, 82 (SD 23); effect 0.96 SD, p=.006. NIT: 72 vs 80, effect 0.76 SD, p=.025. Solved: controls 63.6%, tutored 70.6%, masters 83.3%.
limits: Solve-rate gaps are small and untested here; masters still led. Tests built by the same team.
agent_relevance: Transfer comes from system and strategy knowledge, not from device procedures. Supports a device-independent schema.

source: Gott group (1995) Tutoring for transfer of technical competence: error pattern analysis
finding: The expert-novice difference showed up as premature swapping and wasteful use of self-tests.
numbers: Swaps with no testing: controls 50, tutored 3, masters 8. Self-test used inefficiently: controls 11 of 16 uses, tutored 4 of 12, masters 2 of 14. Violations of logical sequence: controls 21, tutored 9, masters 20.
limits: Counts over small groups (n=21, 17, 12); masters had more sequence violations than tutored, so logical sequence is not a clean expert marker.
agent_relevance: Maps to G2 and G3: measure before you swap or rewrite. Rule: no repair step before a test that localises the fault.

source: Gott group (1995) Tutoring for transfer of technical competence: adaptive expertise
finding: Earlier naturalistic work: good learners used existing device models and a task schema as flexible blueprints for a new system. Weak learners over-simplified and over-generalised old structures and acted like novices.
numbers: Qualitative finding from Gott, Hall, Pokorny, Dibble and Glaser (1992), ten years of fieldwork with F-15 technicians.
quote: They were wedded to their old structures, unable to perceive that the functional variations in the devices in the novel domain were plausible extensions
limits: Narrative report, no counts in this paper.
agent_relevance: Direct for S0 memory: a stored schema must be adapted, not copied. Mark which parts of a retrieved case are device-specific.

source: Parker (1990) Success in tutoring electronic troubleshooting (Sherlock, NASA CP-3059)
finding: Abstract page of the field test of Sherlock at two F-15 wings: tutored airmen gained over controls and approached highly experienced airmen. Gains held six months later.
numbers: Tutored group 16 airmen averaging 28 months experience; control mean 37 months; about 20 hours of tutoring; experts about 114 months; retest at 6 months.
limits: Abstract only (full text could not be fetched). Group size here (16) differs from later reports (18).
agent_relevance: Gains persisted, so the schema was learned, not just primed.

source: Rasmussen (1983) Skills, rules, and knowledge; signals, signs, and symbols (via a web summary page)
finding: Three levels of control. Skill-based (signals, automatic). Rule-based (signs, stored rules, can be put into words). Knowledge-based (symbols, mental model, slow, used when the others fail). Fault diagnosis is a knowledge-based example.
numbers: No experiments on the page. The boundary between skill and rule is not sharp and moves with training.
quote: It is used only when skill- or rule-based performance fails, and the goal must be explicitly formulated
limits: Secondary web summary, not the IEEE paper. Page does not cite Rasmussen and Jensen 1974.
agent_relevance: Gives the S0 gate: try stored rules first; escalate to model-based reasoning only on a failed match.

source: Johnson (1995), after Rasmussen & Jensen (1974) Mental procedures in real-life tasks
finding: Rasmussen and Jensen are cited for topographic search: trace the schematic through a series of good/bad checks. Johnson splits it into forward (from a known good point) and reverse (from the fault).
numbers: Named only; no numbers in this secondary source. Topographic, exhaustive and trial-and-error searches are chosen because little thinking effort is needed.
limits: Primary 1974 paper not opened. Details of the 1974 study not verified.
agent_relevance: Two search modes to implement: match symptom to stored pattern, or walk the signal path.

source: Cho, Funk, Gupta & Yang (2026) Large language models can explain experts better than experts themselves
finding: GPT-4o wrote tacit-knowledge guides from expert behaviour (tutor conversations). Guides built from conversations beat guides written by experts, and shrank the expert-novice gap in a human test.
numbers: Study 1: F(5,605)=35.01, p<.0001; LLM+Conversation beat expert responses by M=0.675 (p<.0001). Study 2: 100 novices per condition; no-knowledge gap 0.843; LLM+Conversation gap -0.088 (CI -0.784 to 0.607); it cut the gap 0.517 points more than human best effort (p<.01). Preregistered.
limits: Math tutoring of young children, one dataset (700 conversations), response quality rated mostly by LLM (Spearman 0.707 vs humans). A gap not different from zero is not proof of closing it (wide CI).
agent_relevance: S0 could be built from expert behaviour traces rather than from experts own descriptions. Fits the experts-cannot-tell point from the Gott group.

source: Oveisi & Manjunatha (2026) LLM-mediated human-AI interaction in search and rescue: impact of expertise on attentional allocation
finding: With LLM help in a grid rescue game, people did more per step, looked less at the game and more at the chat. Expertise moderated the attention shift.
numbers: 13 participants. Victims per step beta=0.02 (q=0.0049); total reward beta=267.1 (q=0.0074); no gain in total victims rescued; mean fixation duration beta=-19.33 (q=0.005).
limits: Only 13 people, one game; the claim that experts keep verifying the AI is in the arXiv listing but I did not see numbers for it. Treat as weak.
agent_relevance: Weak support only. Do not rely on it for the claim that experts verify AI advice.

source: Borchers, Vie & Azevedo (2026) Large language models as students who think aloud: overly coherent, verbose, and confident
finding: GPT-4.1 playing a novice produced think-alouds that were too coherent, too long, and less varied than real students, and overestimated learner success.
numbers: 630 human think-aloud utterances from multi-step chemistry tutoring; minimal vs extended prompts; richer context made the over-coherence worse.
limits: One model, one domain; abstract only.
agent_relevance: LLMs lack the novice memory limits. An LLM cannot easily be run as a novice, so expert-novice contrasts must be built with explicit constraints, not personas.

source: Zheng, Pei, Logeswaran, Lee & Jurgens (2024) When a helpful assistant is not really helpful: personas in system prompts do not improve performances of LLMs
finding: Telling a model to act as an expert in a field did not raise accuracy on factual questions. Best persona per question was not predictable.
numbers: 162 personas (6 relationship types, 8 expertise areas), 4 model families, 2,410 questions. Persona generally no better than no persona; picking the best persona automatically was about as good as random.
limits: Factual questions, not diagnosis. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Warns against you-are-an-expert-technician prompts as a stand-in for a real expert schema. Fits G4 on persona voters.

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench: evaluating AI agents across diverse real-world IT automation tasks
finding: State-of-the-art agents resolved few real IT fault scenarios.
numbers: 94 scenarios; SRE (fault diagnosis and fix) 13.8% resolved, CISO 25.2%, FinOps 0%.
limits: Abstract only; model names not seen. Scores are for end-to-end resolution, not diagnosis alone.
agent_relevance: Baseline: agents without a diagnostic schema do poorly on real faults. Gap to human experts is not measured here.

source: Cloud-OpsBench (2026) A reproducible benchmark for agentic root cause analysis in cloud systems
finding: Final answers overstate how well agents diagnose. They often reach the right cause without the evidence that supports it.
numbers: 754 cases, 57 fault types, 10 agents. Best Joint RCA Accuracy 0.76 (OnlineBoutique) and 0.68 (TrainTicket). Evidence Closure Rate 0.38 and 0.15.
quote: final-answer correctness alone substantially overestimates agents' ability
limits: Metric definitions were not in the abstract I read. Models not named.
agent_relevance: Reason to score the evidence trail, not only the answer. Fits G3: a pass must rest on something the answer was not fitted to.

source: ORCA-bench (2026) How ready are language model agents for oncall?
finding: Agents with real tools and source code still fail most root-cause tasks. Weak ones invent causes.
numbers: 1,079 tasks, five frontier agents. Best accuracy 25.3% on Medium and 10.0% on Hard. Weakest model gave an implausible root cause in 40% of reports. Without source-code access accuracy dropped and hallucination rose for every model. Judge agreement with humans: weighted kappa 0.91.
limits: Abstract only; most models unnamed. A clean public testbed, simpler than production.
agent_relevance: Source-code (system model) access helped every model: a sign that system knowledge is the bottleneck, as in the human studies.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: A 270M-parameter transformer, trained on 15 billion Stockfish-labelled points, plays at 2895 Lichess blitz Elo without search. A learned pattern store can replace search in a closed domain.
numbers: 10 million games; 15 billion data points; up to 270M parameters; Elo 2895 against humans. Perfect distillation of Stockfish not reached.
limits: Chess is closed, fully observed, with a perfect oracle. Faults in real devices are not.
agent_relevance: Shows chunk-style pattern knowledge can be learned at scale. Does not show it transfers to open fault diagnosis.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess
finding: Not opened. Founding result for expert chunking: masters recall real game positions far better than beginners, but not random positions. In electronics, Johnson 1987 cites Egan and Schwartz 1979: experts recall circuit drawings in conceptual chunks.
numbers: From memory, unverified: master about 16 pieces right on first look vs about 4 for a beginner on real positions; no gap on random boards.
limits: Numbers not checked this session.
agent_relevance: Expert memory is organised by meaning. Index S0 by structure and function, not by surface wording.

source: Chi, Feltovich & Glaser (1981) Categorization and representation of physics problems by experts and novices
finding: Not opened (site blocked, 403). Experts sort problems by deep principle; novices by surface features. Johnson 1987 cites the related Chi, Glaser and Rees 1982 finding that both groups hold rich knowledge of the physical setup, but experts add knowledge of laws.
numbers: Details not verified this session.
limits: Physics, not fault diagnosis; effect is on sorting, not on solving.
agent_relevance: Retrieve by function and symptom pattern, not by surface similarity.
